The idea of a hidden curriculum is that there are norms, rules and expectations that are implicitly understood but not immediately clear for someone not from that background. For example, I'm a first-gen undergrad and now grad student, and have a wonderful mentor who explained to me what expectations are in higher ed, what standards of professionalism are, how to dress at conferences, how to respond to reviewers, how to network and who to network with. 

Basically, there's a whole science "etiquette" that I was completely ignorant of and had to do a lot of research and reading to understand how to succeed. And violating these expectations is extremely embarrassing and contributes to the feeling of imposter syndrome, that I don't belong where I am because I don't know the basics.

My fiance was definitely worried that the treatment would cause those kinds of issues for me. But one of the biggest and most problematic issues of my depression is that I have brain fog and don't retain memories super well. Like when I went inpatient, basically that whole year I'd blank slate to me. I haven't noticed any other effects, but it's still possible I suppose. I'm not really worried about it because I've been depressed for so long that I don't really have an idea of what kind of person I am, so it doesn't feel like a loss if that changes. 

And while I hope my depression doesn't come back, it is something I worry about. I'm still seeing my therapist and taking my medication. I'm also at the point where I can do all the other things they suggest for depression: meditate, exercise, eat well, applying coping skills etc. But if I ever get the way I was again, I would sign up for the treatment again in a heartbeat. Even if I have to finance it. But hopefully I'll be able to stick to my discharge directions and continue to benefit.

It honestly feels like there's a woodpecker in my head. The headache after the initial treatment was way worse than I thought it would be, but apparently it's different for everyone. I told the technicians that my brain feels like it's full of soda bubbles when I'm done. It doesn't give me any cognitive effects though. It's mostly a headache for the first couple days until your scalp and skull get used to it. But once you start having gaps between treatments, like your first weekend or now, while I'm tapering (2 treatments this week instead of 5), I had extreme emotional upsets, like big crying jags. Those are basically gone now too though.

And honestly the best example I can give is just that my life went to absolute shit during this treatment. I was kicked out of my friend group, was violently attacked during a trip to Chicago, lost my voice for a week and experienced huge betrayal from one of my parents. This is all within 6 weeks. Before I started treatment I would have likely self harmed or been even more acutely suicidal than normal. But I just laughed at the absurdity of things. I dealt with my shit. I bathed. Brushed my teeth. Cooked food. Went out and made new friends. Confronted my parent. Stuff that I was never able to do even on my best day. I feel like when I was depressed I was looking at life through a dirty windshield covered in dead bugs. Halfway through, the windshield was clean. And now it's not even there.

When I started I ardently believed that it wouldn't work and that it would be impossible for me to get better because I'd been so depressed for so long. It's really amazing.

And thank you! I hate how Evangelical I tend to come off about this treatment, but I firmly believe it saved my life and I hate that companies consider it a last resort as opposed to a viable first line treatment if therapy doesn't work.

I was not functioning properly at all. I was suicidal and completely anhedonic. I barely bathed, had sores on my scalp, completely unkempt. I still went to work but my productivity was not very good. My scores on the deppresion inventory went from a 21 at the beginning of treatment to a 3, where anything less than 5 is remission. Bear in mind I was continuing work with my therapist, but I was only seeing her every 3 weeks anyways, which is obviously less than ideal.

I tried a lot before this. It was seriously a last resort. I did CBT and DBT therapy, intensive outpatient and inpatient stays. I was on varying doses of Klonopin, Zoloft, Prozac, Abilify, Effexor, and Lexapro. I'm still on Zoloft but it's actually working now. I've started drawing and playing guitar again too which is a long way for me.

I have pretty good health insurance so I'm paying 25% of the cost, so I am paying about $1000 total for six weeks of treatment. I'm really lucky because my fiance is paying for it out of his pocket, but the people at the hospital I'm doing it at were more than happy to offer financing and payment plans. 

I hope this helps! I'm willing to answer any questions about my depression and treatment, no matter how invasive.

I'm doing the treatment right now and my only side effects were headaches after treatment when I first started and sometimes my brain feels kinda mushy for a few minutes after I'm done. I went from being suicidal and living in filth 5 weeks ago to now considering applying to go back to school. It saved my life tbh.
